transcript.en: Jill is in LA, and she's worked as a script supervisor. On set, her HSAM was really useful because her job was to make sure that continuity was preserved throughout the film, that someone's hair looks the same from shot to shot, that a table is set in exactly the same way.
transcript.zh: Jill 住在洛杉矶，曾担任过剧组场记。在片场，她的 HSAM 派上了大用场，因为她的工作就是确保整部电影前后连贯不穿帮——保证演员的发型在每个镜头里都分毫不差，桌上的摆设也必须一模一样。

transcript.speaker: Stephanie Foo
transcript.en: And of course, Jill remembered how that table looked, even if the last shot happened weeks ago. I called her up because I wanted to find out if resentment about the past is a side effect of HSAM for anyone other than Joey. Short answer: yes.
transcript.zh: 当然，就算上一个镜头是几周前拍的，Jill 也清楚地记得那张桌子原本是什么样子。我给她打电话，是想知道除了 Joey 之外，对往事耿耿于怀是不是也是其他 HSAM 患者的通病。简而言之：是的。

transcript.speaker: Jill Price
transcript.en: Like, I'm still pissed about stuff from when I was five. And that's ridiculous.
transcript.zh: 比如，我现在还对五岁时发生的事火冒三丈呢。这简直太荒唐了。

transcript.speaker: Stephanie Foo
transcript.en: Jill says she can forgive, but she can never forget. But maybe not being able to forget sort of hinders her ability to forgive as well as the rest of us. Like, she told me she's still angry about this thing that happened in her first year at college, three decades ago.
transcript.zh: Jill 说她能原谅，但永远忘不掉。可或许正是这份“无法遗忘”，让她在某种程度上无法像我们其他人那样真正释怀。比如，她告诉我，她至今还在为三十年前大一时发生的一件事生闷气。

transcript.speaker: Stephanie Foo
transcript.en: Jill had this calendar that she'd used as a diary, writing down details about each of her days in cramped handwriting, so minuscule it's barely legible.
transcript.zh: 那时候 Jill 有本日历，她把它当成日记本用，用密密麻麻、小得几乎看不清的字迹记下每一天的各种细节。

transcript.speaker: Jill Price
transcript.en: Like, written all over. I mean, everything was on there. 1983 was like a really important year. Everything was on there, everything you can imagine. Could be the weather, could be, I mean—
transcript.zh: 就是写得满满当当的。我的意思是，上面什么都记。1983 年真是非常重要的一年。上面记了所有事，你能想到的全都有。可能是天气，也可能是，我是说——

transcript.speaker: Stephanie Foo
transcript.en: Like what do you mean? Like snacks? Like who you talked to? Like, what is everything?
transcript.zh: 你说的“什么都记”是什么意思？比如吃了什么零食？跟谁聊过天？到底都记些什么呀？

transcript.speaker: Jill Price
transcript.en: Everything! Yes, everything.
transcript.zh: 所有事！对，就是事无巨细，全都有。

transcript.speaker: Stephanie Foo
transcript.en: Jill left the calendar at her mom's house for a few months while she went back to school, and the next time she came back, the calendar was gone.
transcript.zh: Jill 回学校上课那几个月，把这本日历留在了妈妈家里，等她下次再回来时，日历却不见了。

transcript.speaker: Jill Price
transcript.en: I can't find the calendar. I'm looking everywhere. So I hysterically go running through the house, trying to get my parents to understand what just happened, how important this was. Like, where's my journal? And they're like, well, we don't know.
transcript.zh: 我找不到那本日历了。我满屋子翻了个底朝天。我就歇斯底里地在家里跑来跑去，拼命想让爸妈明白到底出了什么事、这本日历有多重要。我问他们：“我的日记去哪儿了？”结果他们就回了一句：“嗯，我们不知道啊。”

transcript.speaker: Jill Price
transcript.en: And I remember they had somebody at the house they were talking to, so it was like I was interrupting some sort of a business meeting. But I was also freaking out, and I didn't really care.
transcript.zh: 而且我记得当时家里还来了客人，他们正在谈事情，所以我冲进去就像打断了什么商务会谈似的。可我当时整个人都要崩溃了，也顾不了那么多了。

transcript.speaker: Jill Price
transcript.en: And even to this day, just recently, I said to my mom, you know, I brought that up. I said, "And you did not, you really had no idea."
transcript.zh: 甚至直到今天，就在最近，我还跟我妈提起过这件事。我说：“你们当时根本就、你们真的完全没意识到这有多重要。”

transcript.speaker: Jill Price
transcript.en: She thought I was rehashing things, you know, like, "Why can't you just get—"
transcript.zh: 她却觉得我是在翻旧账，就那种态度，好像在说：“你为什么就不能——”

transcript.speaker: Jill Price
transcript.en: over what happened when you were five. What, what is this, you know? So she couldn't understand why I was bothered or so upset about things that happened decades ago, where to me it was like yesterday.
transcript.zh: 放下五岁时发生的事呢，这到底算怎么回事。所以她根本理解不了，我干嘛还为几十年前的事耿耿于怀、那么难受，可在我这儿，那就像昨天才发生的一样。

transcript.speaker: Stephanie Foo
transcript.en: Why—why is it like super tragic that you don't have that calendar now?
transcript.zh: 为什么……你现在没有那本日历了，怎么听起来像天塌了一样严重？

transcript.speaker: Jill Price
transcript.en: Well, I do have it because I then went back a couple years later and I rewrote the whole thing.
transcript.zh: 其实我现在又有了，因为过了几年之后，我回头把整本日历全都重写了一遍。

transcript.speaker: Jill Price
transcript.en: I mean, I couldn't write every single thing, but I tried to go back and redo the entire calendar. That was how important it was to me. Yeah.
transcript.zh: 当然我没法把每一件小事都写上，但我努力去回想，把整本日历重新补了出来。它对我就是这么重要，没错。

transcript.speaker: Stephanie Foo
transcript.en: And if it's all in your head, it's saved in there anyway, then why bother writing it down?
transcript.zh: 既然这些事全都在你脑子里，反正都存好了，那干嘛还要费劲写下来呢？

transcript.speaker: Jill Price
transcript.en: Because if I didn't write it down, I would have like 50 years of stuff just constantly swirling, and writing it down just sort of relaxes it.
transcript.zh: 因为要是不写下来，我脑子里就会有大概五十年的事情一直在那儿翻腾打转，写下来多少能让人松一口气。

transcript.speaker: Jill Price
transcript.en: And it makes it so that, you know, it's there, it's happened, and it's put away. Does that make sense?
transcript.zh: 这样就会觉得，好吧，事情就在那儿了，发生过了，也就归档收好了。你能明白这种感觉吗？

transcript.speaker: Stephanie Foo
transcript.en: Yeah. It makes a lot of sense.
transcript.zh: 明白，太有道理了。

transcript.speaker: Stephanie Foo
transcript.en: I talked to a number of people with HSAM, and it seems like their days are filled with random memories showing up like bees buzzing around their head until they can get swarmed.
transcript.zh: 我采访过好几位 HSAM 患者，他们的日常似乎总是被各种随机冒出来的记忆填满，就像一群蜜蜂在脑袋周围嗡嗡乱飞，甚至能把人团团围住。

transcript.speaker: Stephanie Foo
transcript.en: By writing the stuff down, Jill manages the memories, like she's taking them one by one, cataloging them, and putting them into a filing cabinet. There's a link between obsessive-compulsive disorder, OCD, and HSAM.
transcript.zh: 通过把事情写下来，Jill 得以管理这些记忆，就像把它们一件件拿出来、编好目录，再塞进文件柜里。强迫症（OCD）和 HSAM 之间确实存在关联。

transcript.speaker: Stephanie Foo
transcript.en: Maybe having the power to remember so much makes you want to obsessively do it all the time. Or maybe it's the other way around—desperately wanting to remember everything gives certain people the ability to do it phenomenally well.
transcript.zh: 也许正因为拥有记住这么多事的能力，才让人忍不住时刻强迫自己去记；又或者反过来，极度渴望记住一切的执念，让某些人练就了惊人的记忆能力。

transcript.speaker: Stephanie Foo
transcript.en: Either way, researchers say, they seem to go hand in hand.
transcript.zh: 不管怎样，研究人员表示，这两者往往相伴而生。

transcript.speaker: Stephanie Foo
transcript.en: About a year and a half ago, I had a really bad breakup. And one of the ways I got over my ex was by managing my memories, which is a pretentious way to say I told myself he was a douchebag.
transcript.zh: 大概一年半前，我经历了一次特别糟糕的分手。我走出这段阴影的方法之一就是“管理记忆”——说白了，这不过是装模作样地告诉自己：前男友就是个混蛋。

transcript.speaker: Stephanie Foo
transcript.en: I dwelled on all the bad parts of the relationship, all his irritating qualities. But recently, I was flipping through some entries in my journal from a few months before it got bad—not for fun, for this story. I'm not that far gone.
transcript.zh: 我反复回想那段感情里所有糟糕的片段，还有他身上所有惹人厌的毛病。但最近为了做这期节目，我翻了翻感情变质前几个月写的日记——可不是为了找乐子，我还没魔怔到那个地步。

transcript.speaker: Stephanie Foo
transcript.en: In one entry, he intuited when I was feeling low and said exactly the right thing. In another, we went to a perfect dinner where we got free dessert. Restaurants were constantly giving us free food.
transcript.zh: 其中一篇写到，他察觉到我情绪低落，正好说了最熨帖的话。另一篇里，我们吃了一顿完美的晚餐，餐厅还免费送了甜点——那时候老有餐厅免费给我们送吃的。

transcript.speaker: Stephanie Foo
transcript.en: We couldn't figure out why, but eventually settled on the idea that people liked us because we just looked so happy.
transcript.zh: 我们一直想不通为什么，最后干脆觉得，是因为我们俩看上去太幸福了，别人才这么喜欢我们。

transcript.speaker: Stephanie Foo
transcript.en: I had, of course, blocked all of these memories out because they didn't fit into the story I was telling myself. And I did not want them back. It had been good to forget.
transcript.zh: 我当然把这些记忆全都屏蔽掉了，因为它们跟我给自己编的那套说辞格格不入。我可不想让这些回忆回来——把它们忘掉真的挺好。

transcript.speaker: Stephanie Foo
transcript.en: And the difference between me and people with HSAM is that I have the choice to stop reading the diary, to just walk away. Jill doesn't have that choice.
transcript.zh: 而我跟 HSAM 患者最大的区别在于，我有权选择合上日记、转身走开，但 Jill 没得选。

transcript.speaker: Jill Price
transcript.en: It didn't like paralyze me until my husband died. Like, his death has really like paralyzed me.
transcript.zh: 以前这事儿倒还没把我困死，直到我丈夫去世。他的死真的就像把我整个人定在原地一样。

transcript.speaker: Stephanie Foo
transcript.en: How is it paralyzing?
transcript.zh: 怎么个定在原地法？

transcript.speaker: Jill Price
transcript.en: Because I will never, ever, ever, ever forget that.
transcript.zh: 因为我永远、永远、永远都不可能忘掉那一幕。

transcript.speaker: Stephanie Foo
transcript.en: Of course, no one forgets their spouse dying. But for Jill, it's different.
transcript.zh: 当然，谁都不会忘记伴侣离世，但对 Jill 来说，这完全是另一回事。

transcript.speaker: Jill Price
transcript.en: I am still in March of 2005.
transcript.zh: 我至今还活在 2005 年 3 月。

transcript.speaker: Stephanie Foo
transcript.en: When he died?
transcript.zh: 他去世的那个月？

transcript.speaker: Jill Price
transcript.en: Yeah. Not every minute, but I could really put myself in that week and feel it and—
transcript.zh: 对。倒也不是每分每秒都在想，但我真的能瞬间回到那一周，真切地感受到当时的一切，然后……

transcript.speaker: Stephanie Foo
transcript.en: So it hurts like it happened yesterday?
transcript.zh: 所以心痛起来就像昨天刚发生一样？

transcript.speaker: Jill Price
transcript.en: Yeah. Now, the feeling that I was not going to survive, I don't feel that way anymore because I have survived, you know? But—
transcript.zh: 是的。现在那种“我活不下去了”的绝望感倒是没有了，毕竟我确实熬过来了，对吧？可是……

transcript.speaker: Stephanie Foo
transcript.en: How often do you think about that?
transcript.zh: 你大概多久会想起一次？

transcript.speaker: Jill Price
transcript.en: Probably like 10 times a day. Even though I get up every day, I feel like I'm still standing in the same place.
transcript.zh: 大概一天有十次吧。就算我每天照常起床过日子，还是觉得自己一直站在原地没动过。

transcript.speaker: Jill Price
transcript.en: It's like—it's really being stuck. It's being stuck in a moment that you can't—there's no escaping it.
transcript.zh: 就像……真的被卡住了，被死死困在那个瞬间里，怎么也逃不出去。

transcript.speaker: Stephanie Foo
transcript.en: Do you wish that you could forget it?
transcript.zh: 你希望自己能忘掉吗？

transcript.speaker: Jill Price
transcript.en: Yeah. Or remember it the way normal people remember it.
transcript.zh: 希望啊。或者至少能像普通人那样去记住它。

transcript.speaker: Stephanie Foo
transcript.en: How do normal people remember it?
transcript.zh: 普通人是怎么记住的？

transcript.speaker: Jill Price
transcript.en: I don't know. But it's not like—I mean, I don't think that somebody would be sitting here 11 years later still like feeling it the way I feel it.
transcript.zh: 我也不知道。但应该不是这样……我是说，我想正常人不会在十一年后坐在这里，依然像我这样痛彻心扉地感受着当时的一切。

transcript.speaker: Jill Price
transcript.en: See, I wish you could understand, and I wish I could understand what it's like to be able to like let things fade and—or not let, just that's the way it is.
transcript.zh: 你看，我多希望你能理解我，我也多希望自己能体会一下，让往事慢慢淡去是什么滋味……或者说甚至不用刻意去放手，它自然就会那样淡下去。

transcript.speaker: Stephanie Foo
transcript.en: Jill says it's not like she's only reliving bad memories. She likes to go back to one of her favorite afternoons, October 19, 1979, in the ninth grade, when she had a bad day at school and her mom surprised her with homemade soup when she got home.
transcript.zh: Jill 说，她也不是光会重温那些痛苦的回忆。她很喜欢回到自己最喜欢的某个下午——1979年10月19日，她读九年级，那天在学校过得很糟糕，回到家时，妈妈悄悄给她熬了一锅家常汤，给了她一个惊喜。

transcript.speaker: Stephanie Foo
transcript.en: But when the bad ones come on, she can't help but get emotional. And they come on all the time.
transcript.zh: 但当痛苦的回忆涌上心头时，她还是忍不住会情绪崩溃。而且那些回忆无时无刻不在冒出来。

transcript.speaker: Stephanie Foo
transcript.en: If you did not have HSAM, how do you think your life would be different today?
transcript.zh: 如果你没有 HSAM，你觉得你现在的生活会有什么不一样？

transcript.speaker: Jill Price
transcript.en: I think that I would have been able to move forward. I think I probably would be married today.
transcript.zh: 我想我应该早就能够向前看了。我想我现在大概已经结婚了吧。

transcript.speaker: Jill Price
transcript.en: I don't think I would be so scared. I would be able to just walk forward instead of constantly looking back.
transcript.zh: 我想我也不会像现在这样胆战心惊。我就能只管往前走，而不是总在不停地回头看。

transcript.speaker: Jill Price
transcript.en: Okay, so let's reverse this so that maybe you understand. So your boyfriend—you guys broke up.
transcript.zh: 好，那咱们反过来打个比方，这样你兴许能明白。比如你男朋友——你们俩分手了。

transcript.speaker: Stephanie Foo
transcript.en: Yeah.
transcript.zh: 嗯。

transcript.speaker: Jill Price
transcript.en: How long were you, like, upset about it, or until the point where you felt like you can move forward without thinking about it all the time, or move forward without it, like, ripping your heart out?
transcript.zh: 你大概难过了多久？或者说，过了多久你才觉得自己可以走出来，不用整天老想着这件事，往前走的时候心里也不再像被活生生撕裂一样痛？

transcript.speaker: Stephanie Foo
transcript.en: Oh, God. Like, three months?
transcript.zh: 天哪，大概……三个月吧？

transcript.speaker: Jill Price
transcript.en: I don't have that luxury.
transcript.zh: 我就没这么好的福气了。

transcript.speaker: Stephanie Foo
transcript.en: And so are you jealous of me?
transcript.zh: 那你会羡慕我吗？

transcript.speaker: Jill Price
transcript.en: No.
transcript.zh: 不。

transcript.speaker: Stephanie Foo
transcript.en: No?
transcript.zh: 不羡慕吗？

transcript.speaker: Jill Price
transcript.en: Nuh-uh. Because on the flip side of all that, I can't imagine what it's like to not remember my life. I really can't understand how nobody does.
transcript.zh: 一点也不。因为换个角度来看，我根本无法想象不记得自己的人生是什么感觉。我真的不明白，为什么大家都记不住呢。

transcript.speaker: Jill Price
transcript.en: Even though it has tormented me, it's just, everything was just—is so important to me that I just, I hold onto it so tight that I wouldn't want to not be able to do that.
transcript.zh: 哪怕这些记忆一直在折磨着我，但所有的一切对我来说都……都实在太重要了，我把它们抓得死死的，我绝不想失去这种记住一切的能力。

transcript.speaker: Stephanie Foo
transcript.en: I'm not jealous of her, either. Ever since talking to these people with HSAM, for the first time in my life, I actually feel just fine about forgetting.
transcript.zh: 我也同样不羡慕她。自从跟这些拥有 HSAM 的人聊过之后，有生以来第一次，我其实觉得能够遗忘真的挺好的。

transcript.speaker: Stephanie Foo
transcript.en: I know that sounds like it's the end of a radio story and this is just what you say, but, like, I cannot stress how sincere I am about this—totally fine about forgetting.
transcript.zh: 我知道这听起来像广播故事结尾时特意凑的升华台词，但我真的怎么强调都不为过，我这话绝对发自肺腑——能够遗忘，真的太好了。

transcript.speaker: Ira Glass
transcript.en: Stephanie Foo is one of the producers of our program.
transcript.zh: Stephanie Foo 是我们节目的制作人之一。

transcript.zh: 本期的节目制作团队包括 Sean Cole、Zoe Chace、Neil Drumming、Stephanie Foo、Chana Joffe-Walt、Joel Lovell、Miki Meek、Jonathan Menjivar、Brian Reed、Robyn Semien、Lyra Smith、Alissa Shipp、Matt Tierney 以及 Nancy Updike。

transcript.zh: Julie Snyder 和 Elna Baker 提供了协助。节目运营支持团队为 Elise Bergerson、Emily Condon、Kimberly Henderson 和 Seth Lind。研究支持来自 Christopher Swetala 和 Michelle Harris。

transcript.en: Music help today from Damian Graef, from Rob Geddis. Special thanks today to Michael Warner and Miles Lock.
transcript.zh: 本期音乐制作协助来自 Damian Graef 和 Rob Geddis。特别鸣谢 Michael Warner 和 Miles Lock。

transcript.zh: 我们的网站是 thisamericanlife.org。《This American Life》由公共广播交换网 PRX 向各大公共广播电台传送播出。

transcript.speaker: Ira Glass
transcript.en: Thanks as always to our program's co-founder, Mr. Torey Malatia. You know, I always tell him, every day is a bowl of cherries. And he always responds—
transcript.zh: 照例感谢我们节目的联合创始人 Torey Malatia 先生。你们知道，我总是跟他说，每一天都像一碗甜樱桃。而他总是回我——

transcript.speaker: Jill Price
transcript.en: Every day is like a bag of garbage.
transcript.zh: 每一天都像一袋垃圾。

transcript.speaker: Ira Glass
transcript.en: I'm Ira Glass. Back next week with more stories of This American Life.
transcript.zh: 我是 Ira Glass。下周同一时间，为您带来更多《This American Life》的故事。
